metadata.title: Error Performance of Relay-Assisted Free-Space Optical Communication Links Over Atmospheric Turbulence Channels
metadata.venue: Proceedings of Eighth International Congress on Information and Communication Technology (Lecture Notes in Networks and Systems)

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This study is a MATLAB-based simulation of free-space optical (FSO) communication performance under atmospheric turbulence and weather scenarios. It does not use any ILSA-style student microdata, sampling frames, or survey instruments; therefore, there are no complex survey weights (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) or replicate-weight schemes to apply. The analysis varies system parameters (e.g., number of relay hops, link distance, receiver aperture diameter, visibility, and turbulence strength) and evaluates bit error rate (BER) against a reference BER threshold. As a result, weighting is not part of the methodology; performance is computed from the physical/channel models and Monte-Carlo/analytical simulation settings rather than from a representative sample.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible Values (PV) are not applicable because the study does not analyze cognitive achievement outcomes from an ILSA (e.g., PISA/TIMSS) and instead models communication-system error performance (BER) from physical channel equations. Missing-data handling is not reported because there is no participant-level dataset with missing questionnaire/test responses; the inputs are deterministic or parameterized simulation settings (e.g., weather visibility, turbulence strength, aperture diameter). Therefore, the concept of missing-data imputation/deletion does not arise in the same way as in empirical survey-based assessments.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: No ILSA or human-subject sampling is used. The study constructs a system model for SISO and relay-assisted N-hop FSO links (N in {1,2,3} relays) and evaluates BER as a function of transmit optical power under specified weather scenarios (clear air, haze, light fog, moderate rain, heavy rain) and link distances (e.g., L = 12 km; also L = 8 km and L = 3 km for aperture-averaging experiments). The simulation settings are summarized in Table 1 (e.g., laser wavelength 1550 nm, responsivity 0.5 A/W, noise variance 10^-14 A^2, receiver aperture diameters D in {20,40,80,150} mm, separation distance rho = 5 mm).

main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using ILSA assessment context not specified in extraction (heuristic migration) the study leveraged the reported predictors to predict Primary study outcome (heuristic migration), finding that This paper evaluates the error performance of free-space optical (FSO) communication links over atmospheric turbulence using MATLAB simulation. It compares a conventional single-hop SISO configuration with relay-assisted multi-hop configurations (N = {1,2,3} relays) and studies BER versus transmit optical power under multiple weather scenarios (clear air, haze, light fog, moderate rain, heavy rain) at link distance L = 12 km, with additional aperture-averaging experiments at L = 8 km and L = 3 km. The key benchmark is a maximum BER threshold of 10^-9 for seamless communication, with telecommunications-relevant ranges up to 10^-12. Results show that SISO can approach outage (BER near 1) under haze/light fog, while multi-hop relaying can reduce the required transmit power by more than 9 dB while maintaining BER ≤ 10^-9 under clear weather and improving performance under haze and rain. The study also finds that increasing receiver aperture diameter (D up to 150 mm) substantially improves BER, enabling large power reductions (overall ~38 dB improvement) for triple-hop links in clear weather. Because this is physics-based simulation rather than data-driven ML on human outcomes, there are no survey weights, PVs, or missing-response handling steps. This indicates that these patterns have implications for educational policy and instructional practice, though cross-sectional ILSA designs cannot establish causality.

data.null_fields_interpretation: The extraction is intentionally sparse because the provided article text is a simulation/engineering performance study rather than an empirical large-scale assessment or an ML prediction paper. It does not train or evaluate machine learning models on a dataset, and it does not use ILSA-style sampling, PVs, or questionnaire-based outcomes. Consequently, fields related to ML techniques and main findings (structured predictive targets) are left empty, while the outcome_summary captures the simulation-based BER benchmarks and system-parameter manipulations.
